newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Survey-better days ahead for East Europe markets.
newsitem.headline: Survey-better days ahead for East Europe markets.

text.p: The outlook is buoyant for East Europe's emerging markets with better credit ratings and growing foreign interest, an economic survey said on Tuesday.

The annual report on European economies by the Geneva-based Economic Commission for Europe (ECE) also predicted Gross Domestic Product growth in the former communist region to rise to an average five percent in 1997 after 3.5 percent in 1996.

The survey, based on statistics provided by governments, said recovery would be fuelled by domestic demand but warned it could be cut short by a slowdown in West Europe, the major market for exports from former communist countries.

ECE economists saw good prospects for the region's securities and equities markets, which international money managers say will enjoy increased cash flows in 1997 from a reallocation of funds away from the rich world.
"New eastern sovereign and corporate entities have entered the financial markets for the first time, and Western institutions are increasingly attracted to the area," they said.
This year, Russia led the transition economies in luring foreign portfolio investments worth $6 billion in treasury bills offering high yields and growing market access, the survey said.
It also noted that the private sector was emerging at the forefront of East European borrowing abroad.
"The amounts raised are still modest but the potential for new issues is considerable," it said.
This year also brought improved international credit ratings, better terms and longer maturities on loans and bonds for the region's borrowers, the survey said.
Hungary narrowed borrowing margins to 50 basis points from 185 while Czech and Slovene borrowers paid 22-25 basis points.

The survey found that increases in credit ratings of 19 east European, former Soviet and Baltic countries this year was more than that of any other regional group of countries -- with Croatia, Slovenia and Estonia leading the way.

The most creditworthy borrowers in East Europe, Poland, Slovakia and Romania, accounted for 80 percent of foreign capital flows of $6 billion into the region in the first half of 1996, down from $9 billion in the same 1995 period.
Poland has overtaken Hungary as the number one destination of foreign direct investment in the region, the survey added.
Foreign direct investments in Poland jumped to $1.19 billion in the first six months of 1996, nearly half of the regional total and up from $366 million in the same period of 1995.

Countries that have reformed fastest were the most successful in attracting foreign direct investments, such as Hungary with $735 million, Russia with $483 million and the Czech Republic with $434 million in the same 1996 period.
By comparison, Bulgaria attracted only $70 million in foreign direct investment in the same period, Albania $36 million and former Soviet Belarus just $8 million.
